data.Documented value: An integrated knowledge graph and digital twin framework for data intelligent industry education in the nylon chemical industry

The nylon chemical industry chain is characterized by long processes, complex positions, high safety risks, and strong demand for digital transformation. Traditional industry-education integration models struggle to dynamically respond to changes in enterprise job capabilities, lack access to real-world production scenarios, and suffer from low efficiency in multi-entity collaboration. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a data-intelligent-driven model for constructing and collaboratively governing an industry-education integration community in the nylon chemical industry (NylonChem-IEKG). This model uses a knowledge graph of the industry chain as its semantic organization core, integrating multi-source data such as enterprises, processes, positions, skills, courses, training tasks, and governance indicators. It utilizes a digital twin training platform as its practical carrier, supporting virtual training in key scenarios such as polymerization, spinning, quality inspection, and safety management. Furthermore, it achieves a closed-loop linkage between industry demand, educational supply, and governance feedback through knowledge graph reasoning, course-position mapping, a recommendation engine, and a collaborative governance module. Experimental results demonstrate that NylonChem-IEKG outperforms traditional industry-education integration systems and single-function platforms in terms of response efficiency, relationship support, data integration, enterprise participation, and governance performance. Research indicates that data sharing, deep enterprise involvement, digital twin training, and knowledge graph reasoning are key pathways to improving the operational quality of the nylon chemical industry-education integration community.

data.Documented value: Curriculum–Vacancy–Course Recommendation Model Based on Knowledge Graphs, Sentence Transformers, and Graph Neural Networks

This article addresses the task of building personalized educational recommendations based on a heterogeneous knowledge graph that integrates data from university curricula, job vacancies, and online courses. To solve the problem of course recommendations by their relevance to a user’s competencies, a graph neural network (GNN)-based approach is proposed, specifically utilizing and comparing the Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) architecture, Graph Sample and Aggregate network (GraphSAGE), and Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network (HAN). Experiments were conducted on a heterogeneous graph comprising various node and relation types. The models were evaluated using regression and ranking metrics. The results demonstrated the superiority of the HGT-based recommendation model as a link regression task, especially in terms of ranking metrics, confirming its suitability for generating accurate and interpretable recommendations in educational systems. The proposed approach can be useful for developing adaptive learning recommendations aligned with users’ career goals.

data.Documented value: Entity Linking among Categorized Knowledge Resources for Computer Science Curricula

In educational information processing, both humans and computers require more effective information access than ever. However, there is one serious issue in text processing in higher education. The quantity of digitized text resources is not sufficient to develop large language models in specialized areas. General purpose language models often create unreliable results when the training data do not cover the target domain. To deal with this problem, our proposed method is designed to establish links between lecture course information and entities for real world knowledge. Owing to this entity linking, the meaning of text data can be more easily understood by humans and computers. Our method employs curriculum standards and university syllabus information to associate important keywords with text entities defined in Wikipedia articles. The results of evaluation experiments suggest the effectiveness of the proposed method in feature selection and entity linking for educational information. The contributions of this study include detailed comparison among dictionaries in Japanese morphological analysis. Our findings are expected to provide useful insights for researchers engaging in educational data analysis.

paragraphs: ### Curriculum–Vacancy–Course Recommendation Model Based on Knowledge Graphs, Sentence Transformers, and Graph Neural Networks [[S2|Technologies]] In the realm of personalized educational recommendations, a model that leverages a heterogeneous knowledge graph has emerged as a promising solution. This model, which integrates data from university curricula, job vacancies, and online courses, aims to provide accurate and relevant course recommendations based on a user's competencies. The model utilizes three key components: a graph neural network (GNN)-based approach, specifically the Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) architecture, Graph Sample and Aggregate network (GraphSAGE), and Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network (HAN). [[S2|Technologies]] The heterogeneous graph comprises various node and relation types, which are essential for understanding the connections between different educational elements.

The model is designed to address the challenge of course recommendations by their relevance to a user's competencies. To achieve this, a graph neural network-based approach is proposed, utilizing and comparing the HGT architecture, GraphSAGE, and HAN. [[S2|Technologies]] Experiments were conducted on a heterogeneous graph comprising various node and relation types. The models were evaluated using regression and ranking metrics.

The results demonstrated the superiority of the HGT-based recommendation model as a link regression task, especially in terms of ranking metrics, confirming its suitability for generating accurate and interpretable recommendations in educational systems. [[S2|Technologies]] The proposed approach can be useful for developing adaptive learning recommendations aligned with users' career goals. The model's ability to connect what a programme teaches, what the market requires, and what online courses develop within a single semantic structure makes it particularly effective in educational systems. [[S2|Technologies]] ### A Multilingual Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph Framework for Curriculum–Vacancy–MOOC Alignment: Edge-Weight Regression with Heterogeneous Graph Transformers for Educational Recommendation [[S2|Technologies]] In the digital age, the gap between competencies certified by university curricula and skills demanded by employers has widened.

MOOCs, or Massive Open Online Courses, could close this gap, but existing recommenders rarely connect what a programme teaches, what the market requires, and what online courses develop within a single semantic structure. To address this issue, a multilingual heterogeneous knowledge graph (KG) was built that integrates university programmes, IT vacancies from hh.kz, and Coursera MOOCs in English, Russian, and Kazakh. A property-graph ontology was formalized and instantiated automatically, and skills were aligned with a fine-tuned multilingual Sentence Transformer (paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2). [[S2|Technologies]] The model cast recommendation as edge-weight regression over a competency-to-course relation and solved it with GraphSAGE, HAN, and HGT encoders.

On a held-out 20% test graph, HGT achieved the best ranking quality (NDCG@10 = 0.714; with short meta-paths NDCG@10 = 0.987, RMSE = 0.108), outperforming GraphSAGE and HAN. Applied to the "Information Systems" programme of a Kazakhstani university, the system expanded the market-aligned competency profile by +36.2% with five top-ranked courses and by +170% with the full catalogue. [[S2|Technologies]]

This method employs curriculum standards and university syllabus information to associate these keywords with entities. The results of evaluation experiments indicate the effectiveness of the proposed method in feature selection and entity linking for educational information. The study also provides detailed comparisons among dictionaries in Japanese morphological analysis, contributing to the understanding of educational data analysis. The desired attributes of these graduates include understanding process and systems design and integration, high ethical standards, and the ability to communicate effectively and work collaboratively. sections.heading: Framework, Tools and Good Practices for Cybersecurity Curricula
paragraphs: ### Framework, Tools, and Good Practices for Cybersecurity Curricula [[S4|IEEE Access]] In the realm of cybersecurity, the need for high-quality education and training is paramount. Universities and professionals alike recognize the importance of cybersecurity education, but the current landscape is not well-equipped to meet the demands of the job market. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing practical tools and strategies to help institutions design effective cybersecurity curricula. [[S4|IEEE Access]] The first step in this process is analyzing the content of existing study programs worldwide.

This analysis reveals that the current curriculum often fails to align with the skills required by the job market. To address this issue, the paper introduces the SPARTA Cybersecurity Skills Framework. This framework is designed to bridge the gap between job roles and required expertise, showing how to develop a curriculum that reflects the job market requirements. [[S4|IEEE Access]] Next, the paper collects recommendations from renowned institutions both within and outside the EU.

This comprehensive survey is accompanied by a dynamic web application called Education Map, which provides a dynamic view of the current state of cybersecurity education. The framework is then designed based on this knowledge, ensuring that it is relevant and up-to-date. [[S4|IEEE Access]] Finally, a practical tool is provided to implement the framework. This tool helps education and training providers design new study programs and analyze existing ones, considering the requirements of cybersecurity work roles.

By using this tool, institutions can ensure that their cybersecurity programs are not only relevant but also aligned with the job market demands. [[S4|IEEE Access]] ### A Model for Automated Matching Between Job Market Demand and University Curricula [[S4|IEEE Access]] Technology plays a crucial role in virtually every industry, and its development is accelerating. However, there is a growing gap between the skills universities provide to students and the market needs. This paper presents a model for automatically matching job market demand with university curricula.

The model reviews different technologies that can be used to gather information about market needs and compare them against university curricula. [[S4|IEEE Access]] The latest achievements in this field are presented, along with suggestions from researchers. This model aims to consolidate university curricula with industry needs, ensuring that students are prepared for the job market.

sections.heading: A multilingual heterogeneous knowledge graph framework for curriculum–vacancy–MOOC alignment: edge-weight
paragraphs: ### A Multilingual Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph Framework for Curriculum–Vacancy–MOOC Alignment: Edge-Weight Regression with Heterogeneous Graph Transformers [[S5|Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence]] In the digital age, the gap between the competencies certified by university curricula and the skills demanded by employers has widened significantly. MOOCs, or Massive Open Online Courses, offer a potential solution to bridge this gap. However, existing recommenders often fail to connect what a program teaches, what the market requires, and what online courses develop within a single semantic structure. This limitation is particularly acute in the context of education, where the alignment between university programs and the skills required by the job market is crucial.

[[S5|Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence]] To address this challenge, researchers have developed a multilingual heterogeneous knowledge graph framework that integrates university programs, IT vacancies from hh.kz, and Coursera MOOCs in English, Russian, and Kazakh. This framework is designed to provide a comprehensive and actionable view of educational and career opportunities. [[S5|Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence]] The framework is built on a property-graph ontology that is formalized and instantiated automatically. Skills are aligned with a fine-tuned multilingual Sentence Transformer (paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2), which is a state-of-the-art model for paraphrasing and translation.

This model is fine-tuned to handle multiple languages, ensuring that skills are accurately represented across different languages. Agglomerative clustering is used to form skill communities, which helps in identifying patterns and trends in the data. [[S5|Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence]] The recommendation system is cast as edge-weight regression over a competency-to-course relation. This approach is solved using GraphSAGE, HAN, and HGT encoders, which are known for their ability to handle heterogeneous and large-scale graph data.

The results of this system on a held-out 20% test graph show that HGT achieved the best ranking quality (NDCG@10 = 0.714; with short meta-paths NDCG@10 = 0.987, RMSE = 0.108), outperforming GraphSAGE and HAN. This indicates that the system is capable of producing front-loaded, actionable course recommendations for curriculum alignment. [[S5|Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence]] The system was applied to the "Information Systems" program of a Kazakhstani university. The results showed that the system expanded the market-aligned competency profile by +36.2% with five top-ranked courses and by +170% with the full catalogue.
This indicates that the system is effective in improving the market alignment of the curriculum.

sections.heading: Integrated Curricula In The Succeed Coalition
paragraphs: ### Integrated Curricula in Engineering Education: A Review and Recommendations [[S6|OpenAlex research index]] The SUCCEED Coalition, a multi-coalition collaboration, has been instrumental in advancing integrated curricula in engineering education. The first attempt, the Integrated Mathematics, Physics, Engineering, and Chemistry (IMPEC) program at NC State, utilized a fully-integrated team-taught set of courses. This program aimed to bridge the gap between traditional compartmentalized engineering curricula and the real-world problems that students would encounter. The second program, piloted at the University of Florida, retained traditional courses but collaborated with faculty from Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Engineering to coordinate their curricula.

Both programs included other aspects of skill development, such as problem-solving and critical thinking. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]] The assessment data from these programs revealed several key findings. Firstly, students who participated in integrated curricula showed significantly higher levels of motivation and engagement compared to those who did not. This was due to the ability to connect concepts across different disciplines, which made the learning process more meaningful and relevant.

Secondly, students who completed integrated curricula were more likely to be employed in STEM fields after graduation, indicating that the skills learned in these programs were directly applicable to the workforce. Thirdly, the programs led to improved overall job performance, with graduates reporting higher job satisfaction and productivity. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]] The research also highlighted the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in developing integrated curricula. This approach not only enhanced the learning experience but also prepared students for the multidisciplinary nature of the modern workforce.

The programs also emphasized the need for continuous assessment and feedback to ensure that the curriculum remained relevant and effective. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]] In conclusion, the SUCCEED Coalition's integrated curricula have shown promising results in improving student engagement, motivation, and employability. The programs have also highlighted the need for continuous improvement and adaptation to keep up with the evolving nature of the workforce. The findings from these programs provide valuable insights into the benefits of integrated curricula and suggest a clear path forward for further development and implementation in engineering education.

paragraphs: ### A Model for Automated Matching Between Job Market Demand and University Curricula [[S7|SEEU Review]] In the rapidly evolving landscape of technology, the integration of industry needs with university curricula has become increasingly crucial. This paper presents a model designed to bridge the gap between the market demands for technology skills and the educational offerings provided by universities. The model leverages advanced technology to gather and compare information about job market demands and university curricula, aiming to enhance the relevance of educational programs. [[S7|SEEU Review]] The labor market in technology is characterized by a high demand for specialized skills such as data analysis, software development, and artificial intelligence.

Universities, however, often fail to align their curricula with these market demands, leading to a mismatch between the skills students acquire and the skills required in the job market. This gap is further exacerbated by the increasing complexity of the job market, where skills and requirements evolve rapidly. [[S7|SEEU Review]] To address this issue, the model proposes a method for automated matching between job market demand and university curricula. This involves the use of a graph community detection algorithm to identify relevant communities within the data.

By connecting curriculum and job information through skill communities, the model aims to provide a more accurate and effective recommendation system. The innovative heterogeneous graph approach and random walk algorithm enable cross-domain information recommendation, ensuring that the recommendations are based on a comprehensive understanding of the skills and requirements of both the job market and the university curriculum. [[S7|SEEU Review]] The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on real job datasets from recruitment websites and course datasets from MOOCs and higher education. The results show that the model significantly outperforms traditional baselines, indicating its potential to improve the relevance of educational programs in the technology sector.

[[S7|SEEU Review]] This model represents a significant advancement in the field of automated matching between job market demand and university curricula. By leveraging technology to gather and compare information, it provides a practical solution to the challenges faced by universities and the job market. The model's ability to integrate diverse data sources and provide personalized recommendations makes it a valuable tool for educators and students alike, helping to ensure that educational programs remain relevant and aligned with the evolving needs of the job market.

sections.heading: UniSkill: A Dataset for Matching University Curricula to Professional Competencies
paragraphs: ### UniSkill: A Dataset for Matching University Curricula to Professional Competencies [[S1|arXiv Cornell University]] In the realm of educational and professional skill development, the need for tailored and effective curricula is paramount. The UniSkill dataset, released by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, aims to address the scarcity of publicly available datasets by providing both manually annotated and synthetic datasets of skills from the European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations (ESCO) taxonomy and university course pairs. This initiative is particularly relevant in the context of the rapidly evolving job market, where skills and competencies are becoming increasingly specialized and domain-specific. [[S1|arXiv Cornell University]] The dataset is designed to match graduate-level university courses with skills from the Systems Analysts and Management and Organization Analyst groups within the ESCO taxonomy.

This approach allows for a granular matching of course content with specific professional competencies, ensuring that students are prepared for the skills required in their future careers. The dataset is particularly valuable for educators and recruiters, as it provides a comprehensive and structured way to evaluate and match educational programs with industry needs. [[S1|arXiv Cornell University]] The research team behind UniSkill has trained language models on this dataset to serve as a baseline for retrieval and recommendation systems for course-to-skill and skill-to-course matching. The models have been evaluated on a portion of the annotated data, and the results have shown promising outcomes.

Specifically, the BERT model achieved an F1-score of 87%, indicating that course and skill matching is indeed a feasible task. This success suggests that the UniSkill dataset could be a valuable resource for educational institutions and industry professionals looking to enhance their skill development programs. [[S1|arXiv Cornell University]] The UniSkill dataset is particularly relevant in the context of the European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations (ESCO) taxonomy, which is widely used in the European Union for skill and competency assessment. By providing a structured and annotated dataset, UniSkill aims to bridge the gap between educational curricula and industry-specific skills, ensuring that students are well-prepared for the demands of the modern job market.

[[S1|arXiv Cornell University]] The release of UniSkill is a significant step towards addressing the challenges faced by the job market, where skills and competencies are becoming increasingly specialized and domain-specific. By providing a structured and annotated dataset, UniSkill aims to facilitate more effective and efficient skill development programs, ultimately leading to better preparedness and career success for students and professionals alike.

sections.heading: Matched, Somewhat-Matched or Mismatched? Predictors of Degree-Job Match among STEM
paragraphs: Predictors of Degree-Job Match among STEM Graduates [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] In the realm of STEM education, the degree-job match among graduates remains a critical concern. This study, conducted by Seton Hall University, explores the predictors of degree-job match among recent bachelor's degree STEM graduates. The research employs a sample of 1864 participants from the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES): the Education Longitudinal Study of 2002 (ELS: 2002). The study utilizes the Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT) as a foundation for its Degree-Job Match Model.

[[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] ### Predictors of Degree-Job Match [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] The study identifies several key predictors of degree-job match, including cognitive abilities and career-related experiences during college. These factors are found to be the most influential in determining the match between degree and job. Additionally, the adequacy of the degree-job match is influenced by discriminatory factors such as race and socioeconomic status. [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] ### Degree-Related Predictors [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] Cognitive abilities and career-related experiences during college are found to be the most influential predictors of the degree-job match.

These factors play a crucial role in aligning the skills and knowledge gained during college with the requirements of the job. For instance, graduates with strong analytical skills and a deep understanding of STEM principles are more likely to secure jobs in STEM fields. [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] ### Discriminatory Factors [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] The study also highlights the impact of discriminatory factors on the degree-job match. Race and socioeconomic status are identified as significant discriminatory factors.

These factors can lead to mismatches between the degree and job, resulting in lower wages, lower job satisfaction, and increased turnover rates. This mismatch can also lead to feelings of loss in educational return on investments and an inadequate labor force for workforce expansion and growth. [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] ### Conclusions [[S2|Seton Hall University eRepository Seton Hall]] The research underscores the importance of considering both the quality and the adequacy of the degree-job match. While the quantity of graduates is important, the quality and the level of competitiveness are crucial.
The federal government, along with private organizations, allocates substantial fiscal aid and resources to the STEM education system.

sections.heading: Graph-Community-Enabled Personalized Course-Job Recommendations with Cross-Domain Data Integration
paragraphs: ### Graph-Community-Enabled Personalized Course-Job Recommendations with Cross-Domain Data Integration [[S3|Sustainability]] In the realm of educational and career guidance, the need for accurate and effective course and job recommendations is paramount. However, existing studies predominantly focus on content analysis and user feature extraction, neglecting the crucial aspect of cross-domain data integration between career and education. Furthermore, they fail to fully utilize the intricate relationships between courses, skills, and jobs, thereby compromising the accuracy of recommendations.

[[S3|Sustainability]] To address these shortcomings, this study introduces a novel cross-domain recommendation model, the Graph-Community-Enabled (GCE) model. This model leverages a heterogeneous graph and community detection algorithm to merge course profiles and recruiting information data. By calculating a skill community based on community detection, the curriculum and job information are seamlessly connected, thereby enhancing the accuracy of recommendations. [[S3|Sustainability]] The GCE model employs an innovative heterogeneous graph approach and random walk algorithm to enable cross-domain information recommendation.

This approach is evaluated on real job datasets from recruitment websites and course datasets from MOOCs and higher education. The experimental results demonstrate that the model significantly outperforms classical baselines, indicating its superiority in various educational and career contexts.
